streams.description: Cross-document event coreference and same-event identity, especially evidence that distinguishes same real-world occurrence from merely similar or related events.
Topic Detection and Tracking, story-link detection, and new-event detection as transfer evidence for CONTINUE-versus-NEW decisions in chronological streams.
Partial, granular, subevent, and non-equivalence event relations that distinguish strict identity from related-but-not-identical events.
Business-process case correlation and process-instance identification when explicit case identifiers are unavailable.
Reject-option and abstaining text classification as transfer evidence for retaining uncertainty rather than forcing assignment.

decisions.reason: The abstract directly frames cross-document event coreference as competition between same-event and different-event hypotheses and explicitly uses coherence, parsimony, and consistency to select between them. That is unusually close to the project's need to establish or refute continuity rather than rely on similarity alone; the incremental graph clustering component also connects identity judgments to longitudinal assignment. The identifier is UNCHECKED, but no verified candidate here duplicates this hypothesis-comparison contribution closely enough to displace it.

The abstract establishes cross-document event-coreference relevance, but only characterizes the evidence as 'rich linguistic features' and does not identify which evidence combinations materially establish or reject identity. Stronger candidates in this set provide explicit analyses of argument evidence, context, discourse structure, or same-versus-different hypotheses, so this paper has insufficient marginal value for the limited reading round.

The abstract directly studies online event detection in a chronological stream, including whether incoming material belongs to an observed event or signals a new event. That decision structure is a strong transfer analogue for CONTINUE versus NEW and provides foundational evidence for incremental assignment rather than retrospective clustering alone. Identifier is UNCHECKED, but the capability is clear from the abstract.

The paper materially strengthens F1 by stress-testing event identity when lexical overlap is deliberately reduced while the underlying coreference links are preserved. The reported degradation on ECB+META is direct evidence that lexical similarity can overstate apparent same-event capability, which is highly relevant to avoiding false merges based on wording alone and to the project's concern about distribution sensitivity.

The paper is genuinely about cross-document event coreference, but its stated contribution overlaps heavily with stronger admitted F1 evidence on discourse/context and event arguments. The abstract does not show a distinctive analysis of which individual evidence combinations establish versus refute identity, so the marginal reading value is insufficient. Its identifier is also UNCHECKED.

The abstract targets the exact binary identity question of whether mentions denote the same real-world occurrence and uses causal intervention plus counterfactual trigger perturbation to separate superficial lexical matching from evidence supplied by event arguments. This is directly useful for the open question of what evidence actually supports or refutes continuity and for guarding against false merges caused by surface similarity. Identifier is UNCHECKED, but the contribution is distinct from the verified candidates.

The abstract confirms a multi-source extraction pipeline containing event coreference, but it does not establish whether the coreference component is separately evaluated or whether the paper analyzes evidence for same-event identity rather than only end-to-end extraction quality. Admit only if the full paper reports standalone cross-document identity evaluation, error analysis, or evidence ablations that materially inform F1 or F10.

The abstract explicitly implements a reject option for text categorisation when first-stage evidence is insufficient and routes rejected cases to a second classifier. Although not an identity task, it is concrete text-domain transfer evidence for preserving uncertainty and performing additional processing instead of forcing an assignment, which maps directly to the project's UNCERTAIN concept. Identifier is UNCHECKED.

This is valid direct cross-document event-coreference work, but the distinctive contribution is multimodal image evidence. That modality is peripheral to the current Outlook/Teams work-matter identity problem, while several admitted F1 papers address more transferable textual, argument, discourse, and robustness evidence. The verified identity does not outweigh the lower project-specific marginal value.

The paper evaluates both first-story/new-event detection and subsequent topic tracking in a temporal stream and explicitly studies combining confidence scores from different similarity measures. That makes it useful transfer evidence for NEW-versus-existing decisions and for combining heterogeneous evidence rather than relying on one similarity signal. Identifier is UNCHECKED.

The abstract is relevant to F3 and usefully notes that named entities are not universally sufficient, but this contribution is substantially covered by the admitted new-event papers, especially the candidate that explicitly separates names, topics, and full-text similarities. With scarce reading slots, this does not add enough beyond that evidence decomposition. Identifier is UNCHECKED.

The abstract establishes the standard detect-and-track news-event capability but does not identify a distinctive mechanism, evidence analysis, uncertainty treatment, or incremental behavior beyond what is already supplied by the stronger admitted F3 candidates. It therefore duplicates the transfer capability without materially strengthening the stream. Identifier is UNCHECKED.

The abstract explicitly separates similarity based on names, topics, and full text for new-event detection. This is valuable transfer evidence for the project's central distinction that shared entities or topic similarity can contribute to continuity decisions without defining identity by themselves, and it provides a cleaner evidence-factorization angle than generic new-event detection papers. Identifier is UNCHECKED.

The paper directly distinguishes full event coreference from partial coreference expressed through hierarchical subevent relations and models them as separate classes. This directly addresses the open gap around strict identity versus subevent/part-of relations and is substantially closer to the required semantics than ordinary binary coreference work. Identifier is UNCHECKED, but the contribution is unique in this candidate set.

The continuum from identity through near-identity to non-identity is conceptually relevant, but the abstract is general coreference semantics rather than event-specific or workplace identity. The admitted subevent paper provides much more direct evidence for the concrete partial-event distinction needed here, so this broader linguistic treatment does not justify an additional reading slot. Identifier is UNCHECKED.

The abstract directly evaluates cross-document same-event clustering and adds document-level rhetorical structure plus dependency-path evidence beyond local mention features. This materially strengthens F1 because it tests whether structural/contextual evidence contributes to identity judgments, an important analogue for the project's need to combine content with source and discourse relationships without equating those relationships with identity. Identifier is UNCHECKED.

The paper is clearly in F1, but the abstract emphasizes X-AMR representation, multi-hop linearization of pairwise decisions, and assessment of LLM judgments. It does not show a distinctive analysis of identity evidence or partial/evolving relations, and its contribution is more about representation and computational organization than the current open gaps. Stronger verified and unverified F1 candidates are admitted.

The abstract demonstrates another capable cross-document event-coreference architecture, but its main contribution is LLM-assisted event understanding and representation learning. It does not expose which evidence establishes or refutes identity, how uncertainty is handled, or how partial identity is distinguished, so it adds little to the specific gaps relative to the admitted F1 papers.

Creating coherent cross-document context is relevant, but this capability substantially overlaps the admitted discourse/context paper and the separate 2025 coherence-and-structure candidate. The abstract does not show a unique evidence analysis, work-domain result, or identity-relation distinction sufficient to justify another slot. Identifier is UNCHECKED.

The end-to-end Dutch CDCR system and error analysis are relevant to F1, but the abstract does not identify a distinctive identity-evidence result beyond positional and graph modeling. Language coverage and generic chain-error analysis alone do not close the present gaps, and stronger papers already cover evidence composition and robustness. Identifier is UNCHECKED.

The paper directly analyzes cross-document event and entity coreference and reports that mention span, surrounding context, and predicate-argument relations each contribute to event-coreference decisions. That explicit component analysis is high-value evidence for determining which combinations can support same-event identity and is more informative for the project than another architecture-only CDCR result.

The abstract clearly concerns one-pass short-text stream clustering with evolving cluster representations, episodic memory, and replay, but it does not say whether an incoming item can create a genuinely new cluster, whether forced attachment occurs, or whether merge/split/retirement decisions are supported. Admit to F4 only if the full method has explicit new-cluster creation or comparable novelty handling and evaluates assignment behavior under stream evolution.

The paper directly studies event-to-case correlation when events from multiple enterprise systems lack explicit case identifiers, using process-model and temporal evidence to assign events to process instances. This is strong transfer evidence for concrete longitudinal identity in an enterprise setting and is substantially closer to work-matter continuity than generic news or entity-resolution analogues. It does not establish Outlook/Teams production accuracy, so its role remains transfer. Identifier is UNCHECKED.

The method combines generated cross-document coherence with rhetorical discourse structure for same-event clustering, but this overlaps substantially with the admitted 2023 discourse-structure paper and other coherence candidates. The abstract does not show a uniquely important evidence ablation or identity-semantic contribution that warrants another reading slot. Identifier is UNCHECKED.

The paper is genuine cross-document event-coreference work, but the abstract emphasizes supervised representation learning, clustering-oriented regularization, and agglomerative clustering rather than evidence for deciding same versus different events, uncertainty, partial identity, or longitudinal correction. It therefore adds less to the open gaps than the admitted F1 candidates.

notes: This gate intentionally does not admit generic CDCR architectures merely because they report clustering performance. The admitted F1 set was selected for evidence analysis, robustness against lexical overlap, explicit same-versus-different reasoning, or structural evidence. No candidate abstract provides direct production-domain evidence for longitudinal work-matter identity across Outlook email and Microsoft Teams, so F2/F10 and gap-4 remain open. None addresses calibration or selective prediction under distribution shift/concept drift closely enough to admit against F9, so gap-7 also remains open. The process-case paper is enterprise-adjacent transfer evidence only and must not be treated as validating msgloom production accuracy. The engineering questions about msgloom's false-merge/false-split costs, CONTINUE/NEW/UNCERTAIN policy, stable identity state, correction model, and bounded retrieval remain project-level experimental/design work rather than resolved literature claims.
